article_title: GitHub Actions Will Block pull_request_target by Default in Public Repositories From December 2, With Brownouts on November 9 and 16

content_preview.title: GitHub Actions Will Block pull_request_target by Default in Public Repositories From December 2, With Brownouts on November 9 and 16
content_preview.summary: GitHub's November 2 changelog says Actions will block pull_request_target by default in public repositories from December 2, 2026, after brownouts on November 9 and 16, unless an event policy allows it.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

According to a [GitHub changelog entry dated November 2, 2026](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-11-02-pull_request_target-blocked-by-default-december-2/), "Starting December 2, 2026, GitHub Actions will block pull_request_target events by default in all public repositories, unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them." The entry adds that "Enforcement was previously scheduled for November 2, 2026." The changelog labels the entry "Retired".

## What GitHub Says...

editor_notes.content_quality: Clear Briefing of about 654 words (within the 300-800 range). Structure follows the changelog (rule, brownouts, options, scope), followed by a clearly separated Related Reporting section and an honest What We Don't Know list. Title is 132 characters (under 150).
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all three snapshots from disk (source-0, source-1, source-2 .html.gz, all HTTP 200, no archive fallback, suspicious_patterns null for all). source-0 (GitHub changelog, Nov 2, 2026, status label 'Retired'): confirmed verbatim 'Starting December 2, 2026, GitHub Actions will block pull_request_target events by default in all public repositories, unless an applicable Actions event policy explicitly allows them. Enforcement was previously scheduled for November 2, 2026.'; the evaluate-mode sentence; brownouts Nov 9 and Nov 16, both 16:00-18:00 UTC; 'failed runs with an error annotation; the workflows won't execute' and 'return to evaluate mode, allowing workflows to run with warnings'; Insights; the two options (keep default rule / explicitly allow in an applicable Actions event policy, with workflow file targeting to allow specific workflows); the 'runs in the context of the base repository and can access its secrets' rationale; scope 'public repositories on GitHub Free, GitHub Team, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud, not GitHub Enterprise Server'; private and internal repositories not affected. The 'block by default' scope is public repositories only, as the article states. The changelog gives no reason for the move from Nov 2 to Dec 2, as the article says. source-1 (The Register, Jessica Lyons, Oct 29, 2026): confirmed 'identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories' (the lead says 'Researchers identified at least 83 attacks...'; the body says Radware threat hunters, with Radware's Gabi Nakibly and Zvika Babo named), 'coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens', the event-triggers-workflow explanation, the quote 'incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code', and the least-privilege/separation recommendation. The snapshot contains zero occurrences of pull_request_target, so the article's statement that the report does not name it is correct and the article draws no link between the campaign and GitHub's change beyond saying so explicitly. Minor note: the article attributes the findings to 'researchers' without naming Radware, which is an omission, not an error. source-2 (StepSecurity, Varun Sharma, Oct 28, 2026): confirmed verbatim 'GitHub is introducing a native egress firewall for GitHub-hosted Actions runners' and 'GitHub's current firewall preview supports GitHub-hosted Linux runners'; the post compares the firewall with StepSecurity's own Harden-Runner, so the article's vendor-comparison label is accurate. The egress-firewall claim rests on StepSecurity alone and is worded as such; no GitHub announcement was cross-checked. Internal link to the Oct npm article checked: that article contains 'alongside the existing pull_request_target restriction'. Independent-source recount: 3 sources; The Register is independent of the subject (1); the GitHub changelog is the subject's own page; StepSecurity is a competing vendor and not independent for the egress-firewall claim. Independence is not required for a Briefing.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every date, time, name, number and quote checked against the snapshots; no discrepancies. Quotes are verbatim (apostrophe style aside).
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and factual; no editorializing. Caveats about the Register campaign and the vendor post are explicit.
editor_notes.originality: Existing Herald articles mention pull_request_target only in passing (npm trusted publishing, 2026-10/16 and related). No prior coverage of this enforcement change or the brownouts.
concerns: Article does not name Radware as the source of The Register's findings (minor omission).
The StepSecurity egress-firewall statement is a single vendor source with no GitHub announcement; the article words it as StepSecurity's statement and flags it as untested.
The Related Reporting section is tangential to the headline topic but is clearly labelled and does not imply a causal link.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, well-hedged Briefing on a dated, actionable GitHub Actions policy change that affects maintainers of public repositories, with a time-sensitive first brownout on Nov 9. Approved. Featured candidacy: 1 - accurate, time-sensitive policy coverage for CI/CD maintainers, but a scheduled enforcement notice rather than a major event
